newsitem.title: USA: Dlr drifts to weaker U.S. close awaiting Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: Dlr drifts to weaker U.S. close awaiting Greenspan.

text.p: The dollar slid to a slightly weaker close against the mark and yen amid uncertainty before remarks by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan and the sale of U.S. Treasury five-year notes, currency experts said.
Greenspan is scheduled to appear before the Senate Banking Committee on Wednesday to give his semiannual testimony on the state of monetary policy and the economy.

"Clearly, the chairman of the Federal Reserve always has it within his powers to do damage to the U.S. financial markets," said Robert Near, vice president on the corporate foreign exchange desk at Bank of New York.
"So, that's clear that the markets are concerned about him tomorrow," said Near, referring to Greenspan's testimony.
Last December, comments by the Fed chairman about "irrational exuberance" in stock markets caused financial markets around the world to tumble, if only for a short time.

With the U.S. Treasury also slated to sell $12.5 billion in five-year notes on Wednesday, currency traders adopted a cautious stance worried any weakness in the bond market could spill over into the dollar.
The dollar ended at 1.6720/25 marks and 121.55/65 yen, down marginally from 1.6740/50 and 121.82/92 at the open.

Initially, the dollar had weakened slightly versus the yen in Asia after the chief Japanese government spokesman, Seiroku Kajiyama, said the interest rate gap between Japan and other countries should narrow.
The Bank of Japan has kept official interest rates at rockbottom levels to help stimulate the Japanese economy.
Still, some traders in New York tended to play down the importance of the Kajiyama comments.
I don't think there was much impact from his comments," said Keisuke Aso, manager of the forex service department at Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi in New York.
Aso pointed out that Kajiyama's remarks were general in nature and that Kajiyama is not considered responsible for policy that effects short-term movements in the foreign exchange market.
Since the beginning of the year, the dollar has climbed against the mark and the yen, hitting a 34-month high of 1.7050 marks on February 18 and a four-year high of 124.82 yen on February 14.
Some traders attributed the dollar weakness on Tuesday partly to the notion that the currency market continues to take a breather after the dollar's heady climb.

"I would say, in general, the market's in a consolidative maybe even corrective phase right now from the recent moves up," said Thomas Arnold, a vice president and chief dealer of foreign exchange at Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank in New York. "I think it's more that than any particular event," he added.

In other trade, the dollar closed at 1.4605/15 Swiss francs, up from 1.4583/88 francs at the open. Sterling slid to $1.6350/60 from $1.6370/80. The dollar closed at Canadian $1.3593/98, barely changed from C$1.3592/97. The Australian dollar ended at $0.7757/62, up slightly from $0.7755/60.
